Despite comparable root-mean-square interface roughness in both series, the Cu-buffer-induced morphology exhibits a substantially larger characteristic lateral periodicity. We propose that the enhanced asymmetry originates from the different spatial organization of interfacial disorder, which modifies the pinning energy landscape and amplifies chirality-dependent thermally activated DW propagation. Our results suggest that engineering not only the amplitude but also the lateral spatial correlations of interfacial roughness provides an effective approach for controlling chiral DW dynamics in magnetic heterostructures.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Engineering antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: A. Benedit-Cardenas, G. Masset, M. Bugnet, M. Martirosyan, G. Steciuk, S. Migot, J. Ghanbaja, L. Pasquier, K. Dumesnil, Q. M. Ramasse, O. Copie
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: In this study, we demonstrate the atomic-scale engineering of antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices grown by MBE on (001)-oriented SrTiO3 substrates. Our work achieved a precise layer-by-layer control, revealing how interface-driven structural distortions can be systematically tuned. X-ray diffraction and reciprocal space mapping confirm both the epitaxial strain state and the high crystalline quality of the superlattices. High-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy further uncovers layer-resolved atomic displacements, where La3+ and Pr3+ exhibit antipolar motions modulated by the superlattice periodicity. The alternate stackings of LaVO3 and PrVO3 yield a unique antiferromagnetic transition temperature, which can be tuned by adjusting their relative proportions. This behavior exists despite the distinct spin ordering temperatures observed in the constituent materials. Layer-resolved spectroscopic measurements reveal that the hybridization of La and Pr 5d orbitals with O 2p orbitals is also modulated and directly correlated to the oxygen octahedra rotations. By determining the orbital hybridization and mapping the cation displacements as proxies, we can visualize indirectly the trilinear coupling between oxygen octahedra rotations and antipolar rare earth displacements. Notably, the interfacial oxygen octahedra connectivity between cubic SrTiO3 substrate and orthorhombic vanadate layers significantly influences the structural distortions. These distortions, almost quenched near the interface, relax over few unit cells, demonstrating how strain and interfacial effects propagate through the superlattice. This study illustrates how artificial superlattices can be engineered to control structural distortions at the atomic scale, offering a pathway to tune the magnetic properties through strain-distortion relationships in perovskite oxides.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Wafer-level growth of p4 mm -textured BaTiO3 films on SiO2-on-Si substrates by RF magnetron sputtering
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Ruyuan Ma, Mingliang Zhao, Yuqi Shi, Wentao Yan, Yang Qiu, Xingyan Zhao, Shaonan Zheng, Qize Zhong, Yuan Dong, Ting Hu
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Integrating barium titanate (BTO) films on SiO2/Si-based platforms is essential for the development of future nanophotonic modulators in photonic integrated circuits (PIC). However, the integration of BTO films on these amorphous platforms is far from trivial. In this work, the direct growth of tetragonal crystal (p4 mm)-textured BTO films on 4-in. SiO2/Si using a magnesium oxide (MgO) buffer layer by a magnetron sputtering process is developed. This work presents a systematic study on the evolution of crystallographic orientation and anisotropy energy in BTO films as a function of film thickness. Furthermore, a detailed analysis is conducted on the growth kinetics of BTO films, with the thickness-dependent evolution of surface morphology and Ba/Ti. Simultaneously, strain-engineered BTO films with a Curie temperature (Tc > 360 °C) are demonstrated. This integration method overcomes the lattice matching limitation between BTO and the amorphous substrate, offering a low-cost, flexible integration approach for next-generation PIC platforms.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Strain Controlled Hydrogen Interstitial Site Preference and Hydride Phase Suppression in Epitaxial Vanadium
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Xin Xiao
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Understanding hydrogen behavior in transition metals is crucial for energy storage and sensing technologies. Here we combine density functional theory (DFT) calculations with in-situ electrical measurements to reveal how epitaxial strain governs hydrogen interstitial site selection and phase stability in vanadium. Our calculations demonstrate a robust thermodynamic preference for tetrahedral (T) over octahedral (O) sites, with the energy difference modulated by lattice anisotropy through strain-tunable H 1s-V 3d orbital hybridization. Experimentally, epitaxial V films on MgO(001) exhibit a critical thickness-dependent crossover: 50 nm films show characteristic first-order alpha-beta hydride transitions, while 10 nm films display continuous solid-solution behavior with complete transition suppression. This crossover is governed by the progressive relaxation of epitaxial strain with increasing film thickness: the 10 nm films retain strong coherent strain that flattens the free-energy landscape and suppresses hydride nucleation, whereas the 50 nm films approach the strain-relaxed bulk limit where long-range elastic interactions restore first-order phase behavior. Finite-size truncation of elastic fields and interfacial electronic reconstruction further reinforce this dimensional crossover. Our work establishes a unified framework connecting atomic-scale orbital physics to mesoscopic phase thermodynamics, providing design principles for strain-engineered metal-hydride systems.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Multifractality in sputtered crystalline and amorphous transition metal nitride thin films
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: K. Anantha Padmanabhan, Kuraganti Vasu, P. Manimaran, M. Ghanashyam Krishna
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: In this work, we present evidence for multifractal growth in Titanium and Niobium nitride thin films on different substrates. Self-similar multifractal structures such as dendrites and multi-branched snowflake-like structures are reported. The fractal dimensions are controlled by a combination of processing parameters and conditions at the film-substrate interface. Significantly, fractal growth is observed not only in crystalline films on crystalline and amorphous substrates but also on amorphous films on crystalline substrates. The 2D Multifractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (2D MFDFA) carried out on the scanning electron micrographs, clearly reveals the multifractal nature of the nitride thin films. The statistical moments were varied between -5 to +5. The Hausdorff dimensions for the TiN films are in the range of 1.65 to 1.79 while it is 1.64 to 1.74 for the NbN thin films. It is proposed that the observed multifractality is due to a competition between morphological instabilities and Diffusion-Limited Aggregation

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Development of an in-situ magnetron sputtering plasma monitoring setup
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Burak Bilki, Mehmet Tosun, Sena Acikgoz
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.source: Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A: Accelerators, Spectrometers, Detectors and Associated Equipment

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Symmetry-guided self-organization of rotational twin boundary networks in epitaxial hexagonal LuFeO 3
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Yixian Song, Zhan Wang, Zan Ding, Fanli Lan, Chen Li, Huilin Lai, Junyu Tan, Fengliang Liu, Changlin Zheng, Wenbin Wang
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Ordered internal interfaces in chemically homogeneous oxide films provide a route for engineering structural complexity without introducing compositional discontinuities. In homostructural systems, rotational twin variants can generate internal boundaries between domains that share the same phase and composition but differ in crystallographic orientation. However, how such boundaries become organized over mesoscopic length scales during epitaxial growth remains poorly understood. Here we show that epitaxial hexagonal ${\mathrm{LuFeO}}_{3}$ $(h\text{\ensuremath{-}}\mathrm{LFO})$ films grown on MgO (001) develop self-organized rotational twin boundary networks composed of two in-plane variants sharing a common out-of-plane $c$ axis. Using a shadow-mask-assisted pulsed laser deposition geometry, we generate a continuous gradient in the local deposited amount across a single substrate, revealing a spatial sequence from isolated anisotropic islands to an interconnected labyrinthlike network within a single growth run. Conventional and grazing-incidence x-ray diffraction confirm that the developed network retains the $h\text{\ensuremath{-}}\mathrm{LFO}$ structure, with no detectable crystalline secondary phase within the sensitivity of the measurements. Azimuthal \ensuremath{\varphi} scans reveal the coexistence of two in-plane rotational variants, while cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy and atomic-resolution high-angle annular dark-field imaging directly resolve sharp internal boundaries between them. Atomic-scale imaging of the film/substrate interface further shows that all observed epitaxial registries correspond to the two hexagonal rotational variants, supporting the assignment of the network to rotational twinning within single-phase $h$-LFO. These results establish epitaxial symmetry mismatch as an organizing principle for rotational twin boundary networks and provide a structural strategy for designing ordered internal interfaces in homostructural oxide films.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Strain assisted multi path domain wall depinning
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Christopher Keck, Shireen Adenwalla
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: The development of magnetic domain wall-based technologies is limited by the stochastic nature of domain wall depinning. While depinning from pre-defined, engineered pinning sites has been extensively studied, often modeled as a single strong pinning site, imperfections in magnetic thin films create numerous uncontrolled weak pinning sites that are difficult to characterize and understand. Here, we investigate domain wall motion in Co/Pt multilayers with perpendicular anisotropy. The data reveal the presence of multiple depinning paths across numerous weak pinning sites, modeled as a simplified Markov process. Strain, in the form of surface acoustic waves, modifies the pinning landscape, decreasing the effective pinning energy and resulting in shorter characteristic depinning times for all paths. The Markov model predicts a depinning probability that varies with strain as the zeroth order Bessel function for all pinning sites, in agreement with the data. Because strain and magnetic field drive depinning via differing mechanisms, the results offer promise as an alternate and effective means of controlling and driving domain wall motion.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Epitaxial integration of GaN $μ$-platelets and thin films on metallic TiN using a hybrid approach
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Philipp M. John, Thomas Auzelle, Pierre-Marie Coulon, Blandine Alloing, Ileana Florea, Mikel Gómez Ruiz, Jonas Lähnemann, Lutz Geelhaar, Oliver Brandt
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: We demonstrate the synthesis of epitaxial, self-organized GaN $μ$-platelets on metallic TiN thin films. To this end, we first nucleate self-assembled GaN nanowires with number densities between 0.01 to 300 $μm^{-2}$ by molecular beam epitaxy. Subsequent overgrowth of these seed nanowires by metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy yields GaN $μ$-platelets with corresponding number densities. The platelets exhibit N-polarity and form an ohmic contact to the metallic TiN substrate. By adjusting the growth conditions during the metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy, particularly the carrier gas and precursor ratio, the morphology of the GaN can be controlled across a broad range. Growth under N$_{2}$ carrier gas and with a 1:1 NH$_{3}$/trimethylgallium precursor flow ratio results in platelet ensembles with broad diameter and height distributions. In contrast, employing an N$_{2}$/H$_{2}$ carrier gas mixture promotes the formation of more homogeneous ensembles with narrower size distributions around a diameter of $\approx$2 $μm$. Finally, N-rich growth conditions under H$_{2}$ carrier gas enhance lateral growth, leading to the formation of coalesced GaN layers. GaN grown under these latter conditions exhibits strong near-band-edge emission, accompanied by only weak deep-level luminescence at room temperature.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Cold-source field-effect transistor with type-III band-aligned HfS 2 /WTe 2 heterostructure
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Shujin Guo, Qing Shi, Deping Guo, Fei Liu, Xianghua Kong, Yonghong Zhao, Hong Guo
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: The cold source field-effect transistor (CSFET) is promising for reducing power dissipation in integrated circuits by engineering the density of states at the injecting source. Existing CSFET designs utilizing Dirac-source metals or p-Metal-n stacks are challenged by Schottky barriers at the metal-semiconductor interface. In this work, a 2D WTe 2 /HfS 2 heterojunction with type-III band alignment is proposed to be an excellent design of cold source and CSFET. The architecture has a high band-to-band transport mechanism by removing the detrimental Schottky barrier issues. Importantly, the proposed CSFET has the same channel barrier modulation principle as conventional MOSFET to enable a high on-state current. Using first-principles-based quantum transport modeling, we predict a very high $I_{\rm on}$ / $I_{\rm off}$ ratio at ∼ 10 10 , a low subthreshold swing below the thermal limit for a wide range of gate voltages, reaching as small as 41.3 mV/dec, at low source-drain bias V D S = 0.3 $\rm V$ . These findings establish a design principles for next-generation low-power nanoelectronic switches leveraging 2D van der Waals heterostructures.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Intrinsic-interfacial dipole coupling and band alignment in a 2D polar MoSi2N4/MoSiGeN4 van der Waals heterostructure
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Pan Zhao, Wenxuan Wang, Yu Liu, Qimeng Li, Mi He, Xiangcao Li, Xiao Tian, Facheng Jin, Zhen-Yi Jiang
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Polarization-dependent electrostatics provides an effective route to regulate band alignment in two-dimensional (2D) polar van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures, yet the roles of intrinsic and interfacial dipoles remain unclear. Here, using first-principles calculations, we reveal an intrinsic-interfacial dipole coupling mechanism in the MoSi2N4/MoSiGeN4 heterostructure. Despite weak net interlayer charge transfer, pronounced interfacial charge redistribution produces distinct dipolar responses in the two opposite polarization configurations. The dipole contributions partially cancel in UP configuration but reinforce each other in DOWN configuration, giving 2D polarizations of 5.70 and 6.16 pC m−1, respectively. This electrostatic modulation reduces the bandgap from 1.93 to 1.49 eV, while preserving type-II alignment and strongly shifting the band edge positions. The DOWN configuration satisfies the thermodynamic requirements for overall water splitting, whereas the UP configuration is unfavorable for hydrogen evolution. DOWN also exhibits strong optical absorption and a corrected solar-to-hydrogen efficiency of 19.58%. These results identify intrinsic-interfacial dipole coupling as a key mechanism governing polarization-controlled band alignment in 2D polar vdW heterostructures.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Pseudomorphic SiGe/GeSn superlattices grown by molecular beam epitaxy on Ge(100)
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Allison M. McMinn, Tyler T. McCarthy, Hryhorii Stanchu, Xiaoyang Liu, Alexander Golden, Martha R. McCartney, David J. Smith, Shui-Qing Yu, Yong-Hang Zhang
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: SiGe/GeSn superlattices with total thicknesses of ∼0.5 μm were grown directly on Ge(100) substrates by molecular beam epitaxy, achieving Sn incorporations up to 11.4% while maintaining pseudomorphic growth. High-resolution x-ray diffraction exhibits well-defined superlattice satellite peaks and distinct Pendellösung fringes in close agreement with simulations, indicating precise control of layer thickness and composition. Reciprocal space mapping shows no detectable in-plane lattice relaxation within experimental resolution, consistent with pseudomorphic growth, and transmission electron microscopy confirms uniform superlattice periodicity, with high-quality growth and very low defect densities. Together, these results indicate that this superlattice architecture can enhance Sn incorporation while suppressing strain relaxation. This behavior is consistent with partial strain compensation between the SiGe and GeSn layers, which mitigates the effects of lattice mismatch and the limited equilibrium solubility of Sn. These results establish SiGe/GeSn superlattices as a viable CMOS-compatible platform for group-IV heterostructure electronics with enhanced Sn incorporation and precise compositional and structural control. Such control enables advanced band structure engineering and provides a promising foundation for concepts such as momentum (k)-space carrier separation for infrared photodetectors.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Shubnikov–de Haas characterization of superconductor–semiconductor heterostructures
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: A. M. Zimmerman, Saeed Fallahi, Sergei Gronin, Tyler Lindemann, Patrick Sohr, Ray Kallaher, Alejandro Alcaraz Ramirez, Georg W. Winkler, Samuel M. L. Teicher, William Cole, Sebastian Heedt, Eoin O'Farrell, Gijs de Lange, Roman Lutchyn, Michael J. Manfra, John Watson
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Hybrid superconductor–semiconductor nanostructures are a central component for research spanning condensed matter physics and quantum information processing. Continued progress relies critically on the ability to characterize, control, and optimize several intrinsic material properties, including spin–orbit coupling, band offsets, and disorder, in a device-relevant stack that necessarily couples the electronic states of a superconducting metal film and a semiconductor. Here, we report a new method to extract fundamental material parameters utilizing simple Shubnikov–de Haas oscillation measurements in heterostructures in which metallic electronic states are coupled to a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) residing in an InAs quantum well beneath an aluminum thin film. Proper analysis of the full magnetoresistance data facilitates extraction of the quantum well carrier density, spin–orbit coupling strength, and both transport and quantum scattering times. Most importantly, the extracted scattering times in the 2DEG are impacted by the metal–semiconductor coupling strength, allowing us to quickly measure an upper bound for superconductor–semiconductor coupling without any fabrication or mK measurements. The wealth of information that is accessed with these simple measurements positions this methodology as an important tool for hybrid materials optimization.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Nitrogen Defect Coupling in Epitaxial LaFeO3 From Structural Reconstruction to Water Oxidation
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Le Wang, Shan Lin, Min-Ju Choi, Krishna P. Koirala, Mark E. Bowden, Jeffrey A. Dhas, Zihua Zhu, George E. Sterbinsky, Tiffany C. Kaspar, Chongmin Wang, Scott A. Chambers, Ho Nyung Lee, Peter V. Sushko, Yingge Du
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Earth-abundant ABO3-type perovskite oxides provide a versatile platform for understanding how anion chemistry and defects govern electrocatalytic behavior. Here, we use epitaxial LaFeO3-xNy thin films to reveal how dilute N incorporation (<0.8% N/O) couples to defect formation, structural reconstruction, and water oxidation. Nitrogen-plasma-assisted pulsed laser deposition introduces N and is accompanied by reduced oxygen content, localized Fe-metal exsolution, and pronounced lattice expansion, while preserving predominantly Fe3+ in the bulk of the film. Ab initio calculations identify a plausible charge-balanced extended defect configuration involving coupled oxygen and Fe vacancies with substitutional N incorporation, reproducing the experimentally observed lattice expansion while preserving the bulk-average Fe oxidation state. The resulting electronic-state redistribution is accompanied by substantially modified electrical transport and nearly two orders of magnitude higher initial oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity than undoped LaFeO3. Under OER conditions, however, the highly active as-grown state is metastable: near-surface N depletion and Fe0 oxidation/removal accompany rapid initial activity decay toward a quasi-steady state. pH-dependent kinetics and post-OER anion redistribution are consistent with possible lattice-oxygen participation. These results establish relationships among dilute anion incorporation, coupled defect reconstruction, electronic properties, and electrochemical behavior in perovskite oxides.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Spin correlations in La3Ni2O7 thin films
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Hengyang Zhong, Bo Hao, Zhijia Zhang, Anni Chen, Yuan Wei, Ruixian Liu, Xinru Huang, Chunyi Li, Wenting Zhang, Chang Liu, Xiao-Sheng Ni, Marli dos Reis Cantarino, Kurt Kummer, Nicholas B. Brookes, Kun Cao, Yuefeng Nie, Thorsten Schmitt, Xingye Lu
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: The discovery of ambient-pressure superconductivity with T c , onset > 40 K in La 3 Ni 2 O 7 (LNO) thin films grown on the SrLaAlO 4 (SLAO) substrate with compressive ( ε ≈−2%) epitaxial strain provides a unique platform for investigating the superconducting mechanism in nickelate superconductors. Here, we use resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to resolve the dispersive spin excitations in the LNO/SLAO thin film and track how epitaxial strain modifies the magnetic spectrum and the $${d}_{{z}^{2}}$$ d z 2 -related high-energy response of LNO thin films with strain ranging from ε ≈−2% to +1.9%. Compared with bulk LNO, LNO/SLAO exhibits well-defined spin excitations with a dispersion similar to that of bulk LNO but with a slightly larger bandwidth, whereas tensile-strained LNO/SrTiO 3 exhibits a marked suppression of the magnetic spectral weight, together with a broadening and suppression of $${d}_{{z}^{2}}$$ d z 2 -related d d -excitation features. Because these d d -excitation features are also sensitive to oxygen stoichiometry, electronic localization, and itinerant screening, we treat them as qualitative measure of the Ni $$3{d}_{{z}^{2}}$$ 3 d z 2 –O 2 p z electronic response. Within a minimal bilayer single-stripe J c − J 1 − J 2 model, the spin-excitation dispersion is described by a strain-dependent interlayer exchange S J c , which is enhanced under compressive strain and substantially reduced under tensile strain. These results provide spectroscopic constraints on how epitaxial strain tunes magnetic correlations in bilayer nickelate films and on models that emphasize interlayer magnetic exchange in this materials family.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Composition Driven Band Alignment Evolution in Grafted Si/GeSn Heterostructures
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Pargam Vashishtha, Samuel A. Haessly, Yang Liu, Tsung-Han Tsai, Kushal Dahal, Shui-Qing Yu, Edward K. Huang, Nanditha M. Dissanayake, Zhenqiang Ma
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Understanding and controlling band alignment in lattice-mismatched group-IV semiconductor-based heterostructures is fundamental to rational band-structure engineering, as it governs the electronic structure and carrier transport in heterointegrated semiconductor systems. Despite growing interest in Si/GeSn heterostructures, the composition-dependent band alignment has not been experimentally established. Here, we experimentally establish the evolution of band alignment in semiconductor-grafted Si/GeSn heterostructures with contents ranging from 8.8% to 12.4% using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and Kraut's core-level method. The valence-band offset increases systematically from ~0.29 to ~0.57 eV with increasing Sn composition, whereas the corresponding effective conduction-band offset decreases from ~0.30 to ~0.12 eV. The observed band-alignment evolution is attributed to an upward shift of the GeSn valence-band maximum arising from enhanced p-p orbital hybridization, reduced bonding-antibonding splitting, and compressive-strain-induced heavy-hole band lifting. These findings establish the experimental relationship between alloy composition and interfacial band alignment in semiconductor-grafted Si/GeSn heterostructures, providing a quantitative framework for rational band-structure engineering in lattice-mismatched group-IV semiconductor heterostructures.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Scalable operating currents in amorphous W-N/FePt superconducting rectifiers
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: S. Russo, A. Sanson, Yeonkyu Lee, Jeehoon Kim, N. Haberkorn
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: We demonstrate high-efficiency, field-free superconducting diode behavior in W-N/FePt bilayers fabricated entirely by sputtering at room temperature. The devices combine amorphous W-N superconducting thin films with a 48-nm-thick FePt layer exhibiting remanent stripe-domain magnetization. We used lithographically patterned microbridges to compare W-N/FePt bilayers with single-layer W-N reference films at three nominal W-N thicknesses (18, 24, and 28 nm). The bilayers exhibit superconducting transition temperatures of approximately 4.1-4.3 K. At zero applied magnetic field, the current-voltage (I-V) characteristics exhibit pronounced nonreciprocity, controlled by the orientation of the in-plane remanent FePt magnetization relative to the transport current. The diode response is maximized for perpendicular alignment, reverses polarity upon magnetization reversal, and is strongly suppressed when the magnetization is aligned with the current. This behavior is consistent with asymmetric vortex entry and motion governed by the magnetic stray fields generated near the bridge edges. At 3 K with the remanent magnetization perpendicular to the current, increasing the W-N thickness from 18 to 28 nm widens the current interval between the dissipation thresholds for opposite polarities from about 0.3 to 1.55 mA. All three bilayers exhibit diode efficiencies of approximately 75-80% in this configuration.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Bayesian inference of burn history metrics measured with the particle time of flight (PTOF) detector at the National Ignition Facility
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Y. Lawrence, E. Edwards, C. W. Wink, T. E. Evans, B. L. Reichelt, N. Izumi, S. Palaniyappan, G. D. Sutcliffe, E. Mariscal, T. Nguyen, D. Schlossberg, R. D. Petrasso, M. Gatu Johnson, C. K. Li, J. A. Frenje
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: The particle time-of-flight (PTOF) detector is a chemical vapor deposition diamond detector used on low yield shots (≲1015 neutrons) at the National Ignition Facility (NIF) to measure the time of peak nuclear emission. Burn widths and burn histories can also be measured if the detector response is sufficiently fast compared to the burn width. Standard analysis techniques use maximum-likelihood-based forward fits or deconvolution techniques. While generally sufficient, it can be difficult to rigorously quantify all chosen sources of uncertainty, and for burn history measurements, deconvolution methods are limited by measurement noise, making rigorous uncertainty quantification challenging. Here, a Bayesian inference framework with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling is described and applied to several NIF experiments to highlight its benefits. These include rigorous error quantification for all analyzed signals, clearer interpretation of relatively complex PTOF signals such as those with overlapping particle arrival histories, and inference of nuclear burn histories.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Divide-and-conquer neural-network surrogates for quantum sampling: Accelerating Markov-chain Monte Carlo in large-scale constrained optimization problems
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Yuya Kawamata, Yuichiro Nakano, Keisuke Fujii
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) [D.~Layden \mbox{\textit{et al.}},\href{https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06095-4} {Nature 619, 282--287 (2023)}] is a promising way to use quantum-circuit samples as MCMC proposals to improve sampling efficiency. On the other hand, many practical problems are large-scale and constrained, making it difficult to construct efficient proposal distributions in classical methods and slowing down MCMC mixing. In this work, we propose a divide-and-conquer neural network surrogate framework for quantum sampling to accelerate MCMC under fixed Hamming weight constraints. Our method divides the interaction graph for an Ising problem into subgraphs, generates samples using QAOA for those subproblems with an XY mixer, and trains neural network surrogates conditioned on the Hamming weight to provide proposal distributions for each subset while preserving the constraint. In numerical experiments of Boltzmann sampling on 3-regular graphs, our method consistently accelerated mixing as the system size $N$ increased, with average improvements in the autocorrelation decay rate constant by speedup factors of about \mbox{$14.0$} and \mbox{$7.7$} over local and global Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. We also applied the method to an MNIST feature mask optimization problem with $N=784$, obtaining faster energy convergence and a classification accuracy 2.03 percentage points higher than that of global Kawasaki dynamics after 50 MCMC steps. These numerical results support the usefulness of surrogate proposals with a divide-and-conquer strategy for large-scale constrained sampling and finite-step optimization.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Bayesian inference with a polymer probabilistic computer
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Travis Wanless, Yuriy Bandera, Lubomir Kostal, Stephen H. Foulger
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Bayesian inference weighs competing explanations of noisy data by sampling from a posterior distribution, a task that deterministic hardware performs only by simulating randomness. Probabilistic bits (p-bits) supply this randomness physically, but the few hardware networks of p-bits built so far use inorganic devices, address optimization or learning, and are judged without reference to the spread expected from finite sampling. Here we report a probabilistic computer built from solution-processed conjugated-polymer memristors. Four polymer p-bits, tracked online for drift and coupled in a closed Gibbs-sampling loop, sample competing, degenerate and cooperative posteriors over sixteen states with statistics that fall within the range of ideal p-bits, both in their distribution and in their autocorrelation, without any parameter fitted to the target. This agreement extends to new simulated sensor readings whose outcome was predicted before each run, including readings that point away from the true answer. Reprogrammed in software, the same circuit and controller reproduces the invertible AND gate of earlier p-bit networks, with its temperature fixed in advance rather than fitted. Polymer p-bits thus open a route to printed, large-area probabilistic computers that infer alongside their sensors.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Digital least-squares amplitude detection for high-speed atomic force microscopy
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: High-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM) in amplitude-modulated (tapping) mode requires rapid and reliable amplitude detection for real-time feedback control. Here, we develop a low-latency field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-based digital least-squares (LSQ) amplitude detector for HS-AFM operation. Although LSQ is a well-established signal-processing method, the novelty of this work lies in its implementation as a high-frequency, microsecond-response amplitude detector for real-time HS-AFM feedback. To enable real-time operation, we implemented a two-parameter LSQ formulation on FPGA hardware, in which the adjustable fitting-window length defines the number of sampled points used for each amplitude estimate. We evaluated LSQ using numerical simulations, signal-generator measurements, HS-AFM deflection-signal analysis, and biological HS-AFM imaging. Under matched response-time conditions, numerical simulations showed that LSQ produced amplitude-estimate fluctuations comparable to Fourier-amplitude-based detection and lower than those produced by sample-and-hold-based detection (SHB) and phase-shift-based detection. Experimental measurements further showed that shorter LSQ windows provided SHB-like response times, whereas longer windows reduced amplitude-estimate fluctuations. LSQ also supported stable HS-AFM imaging of annexin-V lattices on supported lipid bilayers. These results establish digital LSQ as an additional amplitude-detection strategy for HS-AFM, particularly for applications involving noisy cantilever deflection signals where tunable control of the response-time/amplitude-fluctuation trade-off is needed.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Particle transport studies using gas puff modulation and multi-channel heterodyne interferometry in the Helically Symmetric eXperiment
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: D. Damaskopoulos, H. O. M. Hillebrecht, G. Tryfonos, M. D. Nornberg, W. R. Goodman, B. Geiger
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Understanding and controlling particle transport in future power plants is critical, as peaked density profiles are needed for high-density operation and reduced turbulent heat fluxes. Here, we determine particle transport coefficients in density-modulation experiments on the Helically Symmetric eXperiment stellarator, using a multi-channel heterodyne interferometer (IF) and a multi-profile Thomson Scattering (TS) diagnostic. We perform parameter fitting with Bayesian inference and the pySTRAHL code to forward-model densities. Fitting is done with three routines: an IF-only, a TS-only, and an integrated data analysis (IDA) routine. Fitting with the IF yields peaked density profiles with diffusion values ≈2.5m2/s over much of the mid-radius and inward convection (V < 0), ranging from −10 to −50 m/s. The TS routine constrains the density profile shape and reveals minor core hollowing, but does not constrain its magnitude or distinguish transport coefficients. The IDA fit yields small core diffusion (D ≈ 0.01 m2/s) limited by the bounds of the prior distribution and increases toward the edge, approaching Bohm-scaling values. Small outward convection in the core suggests minor hollowing. Between 0.1 ≲ r/a ≲ 0.85, an inward pinch is observed, which then flips outward at r/a ≈ 0.85 with large uncertainty bands throughout. The hollowing in the TS-only and IDA fits conflicts with the peaked profiles suggested by the IF. These results highlight modulation studies, combined with fast density measurements, as a tool for studying diffusive and convective particle transport in the Helically Symmetric eXperiment.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: quantEM: Quantitative Electron Microscopy Analysis from Differentiable Physics to Neural Priors
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Colin Ophus, Arthur RC McCray, Georgios Varnavides, Stephanie M Ribet
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Quantitative electron microscopy includes imaging, diffraction, spectroscopy, and tomography measurements, and the analysis of these measurements increasingly requires solving inverse problems with physical forward models. Open-source software has made many of these analyses widely available, but most packages are organized around a single modality, so that multimodal analyses require moving data between packages, and new methods cannot easily reuse the physical models and optimizers of existing ones. Here we present quantEM, an open-source Python package for quantitative electron microscopy that uses PyTorch tensors for computation and automatic differentiation, and Zarr for storage. We implement each analysis method by writing a differentiable forward model and choosing a representation, loss function, constraints, and optimizer from a library of components, so that every method runs on CPUs and GPUs, can be saved and resumed, and uses the same calibrated data structures and visualization tools. We describe the current modules, including orientation and strain mapping, direct and iterative ptychography, tomography with neural representations, and X-ray and electron energy-loss spectroscopy, and show how we assemble combined methods such as ptychographic tomography from existing components. quantEM is available under the MIT license, together with documentation, tutorials, and curated example datasets.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Real-axis least-squares bath discretization for real-time transport in quantum-dot Josephson junctions
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Ruixin Zhou, Bing Dong, Yiyan Wang

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Sobolev theory for the inverse problem of time-dependent density functional theory on the torus
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Asbjørn Bækgaard Lauritsen, Mathieu Lewin, Jakob Oldenburg
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: We show that, given a sufficiently regular time-dependent density, there exists a unique potential such that the Schrödinger equation with this external potential has the prescribed one-particle density. We treat densities that are twice differentiable in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space; the resulting potentials are continuous in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space. Our method of proof is to rewrite the problem as a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a loss of derivatives, which we in turn handle with a completion-of-the-square argument. This is a refinement of our recent work [Lauritsen, Lewin, and Oldenburg, arXiv:2609.08984], which handled this loss of derivatives using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem and treated analytic-in-space densities and potentials.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Hyperkagome antiferromagnetism in the iron garnet Almandine Fe$_3$Al$_2$Si$_3$O$_{12}$
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Minnong Zhang, Harald O. Jeschke, Daniel Guterding
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Antiferromagnets on the hyperkagome lattice provide a three-dimensional route to strong magnetic frustration, but experimentally accessible realizations with well-established microscopic Hamiltonians remain scarce. Garnets are a broad family of materials in which magnetic ions can form two interpenetrating hyperkagome lattices, giving rise to spin glass, spin-liquid and hidden-order physics. Here we identify the iron aluminosilicate garnet almandine, Fe$_3$Al$_2$Si$_3$O$_{12}$, as a spin-$2$ hyperkagome antiferromagnet. Using density functional theory energy mapping, we determine a Heisenberg Hamiltonian for the high-spin Fe$^{2+}$ moments and find dominant nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic exchange, as well as significant longer-range interactions. Classical Monte Carlo simulations of this Hamiltonian, combined with quantum-to-classical rescaling of the spin length, show a transition to antiferromagnetic order at $T_{\rm N}\approx9.8$K, in excellent agreement with specific heat experiments. The resulting non-collinear magnetic state is naturally described by magnetic toroidal octupolar order, which we connect to known results for the highly frustrated hyperkagome antiferromagnet gadolinium gallium garnet, Gd$_3$Ga$_5$O$_{12}$. We also calculate magnetic neutron diffraction amplitudes as well as static and dynamic structure factors using semiclassical dynamics, providing quantitative predictions for future neutron scattering experiments. Our results establish almandine as a chemically accessible realization of frustrated hyperkagome magnetism in the garnet family.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Chiral Superconductivity Indifferent to Parent Topology in the Square-Lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard Model
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Jia-Xin Zhang, Wen O. Wang, Leon Balents, Lucile Savary, D. N. Sheng
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: We study a $π$-flux square-lattice $t$-$t'$ Hofstadter-Hubbard model proposed to be realizable in twisted moiré bilayers. By tuning $U$ and $t'$ at half filling, ground-state density-matrix renormalization group simulations (DMRG) and a parton analysis identify an integer quantum Hall (IQH) phase, a chiral spin liquid (CSL), and an antiferromagnet (AFM) in the phase diagram, while charge and spin fluctuations from finite-temperature determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) suggest a closing charge gap but an open spin gap at the IQH-CSL boundary, consistent with the topological criticality expected there. This model therefore produces a phase diagram hosting weakly correlated band topology (IQH), intrinsic topological order (CSL), and conventional symmetry breaking (AFM) side by side. Upon doping any of these three parent phases, a single chiral topological superconductor with spin Chern number $C_s=-2$ occupies nearly the entire phase diagram. DMRG, DQMC, and weak-coupling perturbation theory agree on its pairing symmetry. This shows that doping the topological band of our model robustly induces the same paired state throughout the phase diagram regardless of the character of the underlying correlated half-filled state and its magnetic fluctuations, whether an IQH, a spin liquid or a weakly fluctuating AFM.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Fast Accurate Quantum Monte Carlo without Metropolis Adjustment
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Reuben Cohn-Gordon, Gabriel Pescia, Sumner N. Hearth, Jakob Robnik, Uroš Seljak, Peter Lunts
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: In quantum systems, physical quantities of interest can be expressed as expectation values of a probability distribution, which allows their estimation by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. This approach, an instance of Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC), plays a central role in obtaining predictions of system properties relevant to condensed matter and high energy physics. The use of Hamiltonian dynamics to design a Markov kernel, known as Hybrid or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), is widespread in quantum applications. In this context, it is standard to use an HMC kernel that is ``adjusted'' with the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) criterion, so that estimates of expectations converge to their true value in the limit of infinite sample size. However, recent work in computational statistics suggests that an \emph{unadjusted} HMC kernel can be significantly more efficient, while safely maintaining an asymptotic bias which is small relative to the error arising from the variance of the finite sample size. We adapt this approach to the QMC setting, focusing on a challenging and high-dimensional \emph{spin-fermion} model of a quantum phase transition. We find that unadjusted methods outperform adjusted HMC in terms of effective sample size per gradient call, while retaining accurate results.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Mott transitions in Dirac nodal-line semimetals
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Andressa R. Medeiros-Silva, Lucas O. Lima, Marcello B. da Silva Neto, Fakher F. Assaad, Natanael C. Costa
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Nodal-line semimetals provide a natural setting to investigate how the geometry of a nodal manifold affects interaction-driven quantum phase transitions. Here, we study the Hubbard model on a cubic lattice supporting either nodal-point (cubic $π$-flux model) or nodal-line semimetallic states using mean-field theory, determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations, and a weak-coupling renormalization-group (RG) analysis. In both cases, antiferromagnetic order develops only above a finite interaction strength, with the nodal-line system exhibiting a smaller critical coupling due to its enhanced low-energy density of states and markedly stronger finite-size effects. For the nodal-point model, the quantum critical behavior is compatible with $(3+1)$-dimensional Gross--Neveu mean-field scaling. In contrast, the weak-coupling RG reveals that the nodal line itself is unstable against interactions: although the Hubbard interaction is perturbatively irrelevant, its second-order self-energy generates a symmetry-allowed relevant term proportional to $U^2\cos k_z$, reconstructing the nodal line into isolated, strongly anisotropic nodal points. This weak-coupling reconstruction is distinct from the strong-coupling antiferromagnetic transition and highlights the role of nodal-manifold geometry in interacting semimetals.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Quantum benchmarks for magnetic energies and transition temperatures
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Mojtaba Alaei, Ilia Mikhailov, Alireza Qaiumzadeh, Artem Oganov
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Predicting magnetic ordering temperatures requires accurate exchange interactions and an appropriate treatment of spin thermodynamics. Here we assess these requirements through complementary quantum Monte Carlo benchmarks. For five insulating antiferromagnets, we compare ferromagnetic-antiferromagnetic energy differences from diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) and density functional theory with references reconstructed from inelastic neutron scattering (INS) exchanges. DMC underestimates these references but achieves a mean absolute error comparable to the best-performing functionals tested. Separately, we directly test the previously proposed (S+1)/S rescaling of classical Monte Carlo temperatures against quantum stochastic series expansion simulations for 17 compounds using corresponding INS-derived Heisenberg Hamiltonians. Rescaling reduces the mean absolute classical-quantum temperature difference from 81.7 to 8.2 K, with a mean absolute percentage difference of 5.9 %. These results establish a direct quantum benchmark for the rescaling within the tested models and emphasize that improvements in electronic magnetic energy scales should be accompanied by attention to quantum spin thermodynamics.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Excitonic order tuned by electric fields and driven by interorbital Coulomb interactions in twisted bilayer graphene
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Shi-Chao Fang, Xin-Yi Liao, Jing Fan, Pu-Yan Yin
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Excitonic order, as a representative electronic instability in strongly correlated systems, has attracted significant attention in moiré systems. In this work, we investigate the emergence and tunability of excitonic order in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) within an effective two-orbital Hubbard model, using large-scale constrained-path quantum Monte Carlo simulations. We demonstrate that the excitonic correlations are significantly enhanced by the external electric field ε , the inter-orbital Coulomb interaction V ⊥ , and the inter-orbital hopping t ⊥ . By analyzing both short-range and long-range excitonic correlation functions across different lattice sizes, we find that long-range excitonic correlations are robust against finite-size effects and provide reliable evidence for excitonic condensation. Furthermore, we reveal a clear interplay between magnetic order and excitonic order. The spin structure factor shows that increasing ε , V ⊥ , and t ⊥ suppresses the antiferromagnetic order, indicating that excitonic order emerges as a competing instability with magnetism. Among these factors, the external electric field plays the dominant role in destabilizing antiferromagnetism and promoting excitonic correlations. Our results establish a unified physical picture in which excitonic order in TBG can be effectively controlled by tuning interlayer coupling and external fields, providing a promising route for realizing excitonic condensation in strongly correlated moiré systems.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory on a triangular lattice: deconfined fermions in a vison crystal and superfluidity
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Welberth Kennedy, João C. Inácio, Fakher F. Assaad
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: We investigate an unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory coupled to fermions on the triangular lattice at half filling, using auxiliary field quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The triangular geometry gives rise to a global $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry that acts as an Ising symmetry on the plaquette fluxes. At weak transverse field $h$, this symmetry is spontaneously broken, stabilizing a vison crystal. We argue that this phase is deconfined: fermions, charged under an emergent $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge field, propagate in an ordered $π$-flux background and form a Dirac semimetal. Increasing the transverse field triggers a first-order quantum phase transition to a confined $s$-wave superfluid, at which confinement and global symmetry breaking occur simultaneously. This contrasts with the square lattice, where the corresponding transition is continuous. We extend our analysis to finite temperature and determine the thermal phase boundaries of both ordered phases. The superfluid melts through a Kosterlitz--Thouless transition, whereas the vison crystal undergoes a thermal Ising transition. Together, our results establish the $T \times h$ phase diagram and demonstrate how the triangular geometry leads to qualitative changes in both the phases and the criticality of the model.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Correlated Mott semimetal in a one-dimensional SU(2) symmetric topological heavy fermion model
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Emile Pangburn, Igor de Melo Froldi, Anurag Banerjee
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: The topological heavy-fermion model provides a minimal framework for describing the coexistence of localized moments and itinerant Dirac electrons in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG). Several analytical and numerical methods have been applied to this model; however, whether they provide a realistic description of MATBG remains incompletely understood. In this work, we develop an Hubbard operator approach that incorporates non-local correlations beyond the single-site limit. We benchmark the approximate calculations against numerically exact determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations of a SU(2)$ symmetric lattice-regularized model. We show that commonly used local approximations, such as Hubbard-I, fail to capture the coupling between localized and itinerant degrees of freedom, leading to incorrect spectral properties in the local-moment regime. In contrast, the Hubbard operator method provides a better description of both correlation functions and spectral features over a regime of parameters, in good agreement with exact numerical methods.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Dopant Cluster Engineering for Tunable Room-Temperature Ferromagnetism in 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Shivangee, Sachin Grewal, Akash Singh
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (2D-TMDs) offer a promising platform for realizing dilute magnetic semiconductors. However, simultaneously achieving large magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) and high Curie temperature (T$_\text{c}$) remains a major challenge. In this work, we employ DFT+U to systematically investigate the thermodynamic stability and magnetic properties of 2D-MoSe$_2$ and 2D-WSe$_2$ doped with transition metal atoms. We found that the paired dopant configurations are more stable than previously attributed isolated dopants. Despite their nearly identical crystal structures, 2D-MoSe$_2$ and 2D-WSe$_2$ show contrasting properties upon doping. All paired dopants in 2D-MoSe$_2$ exhibit long-range ferromagnetic coupling (FMC) primarily due to carrier-mediated exchange interactions, whereas those in 2D-WSe$_2$ show weak exchange coupling. Interestingly, 2Mn$_\text{2W}$ shows a transition from less stable antiferromagnetic coupling (AFMC) in the short range to highly stable FMC in the long-range. The combined effect of spin-orbit coupling, exchange interactions, and orbital hybridization gives rise to a large MAE with maximum in-plane values of $-$3.5 meV for 2V$_\text{2Mo}$ and $-$3.2 meV for 2Mn$_\text{2W}$. Monte Carlo simulations estimate T$_\text{c}$ $\simeq$ 440 K for 2Fe$_\text{2Mo}$ and ensure its high-temperature stability in 2D-MoSe$_2$. Our results establish dopant clustering as an effective route to engineer high-temperature ferromagnetism in 2D-TMDs and highlight their potential for nano-spintronic applications.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Disentangling Multiple Scaling Dimensions via Operator Covariance in Critical Quantum Spin Systems
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Zhi Lin, Anders W. Sandvik
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: We present a general proof of different power-law decays versus distance of the eigenvalues of two-point covariance matrices in critical lattice quantum models, allowing extraction of multiple scaling dimensions. We demonstrate the practical utility of this method in the context of a spin-1/2 chain with critical ground state described by the SU(2)_1 Wess--Zumino--Witten field theory. Using quantum Monte Carlo simulations to compute covariance matrices in different symmetry sectors, we resolve the expected relevant and marginal primary operators as well as some descendants. The covariance method can be integrated into many existing numerical schemes and promises to significantly enhance computational studies of quantum criticality.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Lefschetz-Thimble Method to the Sign Problem in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev Model
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Yin-Hao Fang, Yang Qi
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: The sign problem in path integrals severely limits the application of quantum Monte Carlo methods to strongly correlated systems, whereas the Lefschetz-thimble method offers a rigorous framework to mitigate this issue. In this paper, we establish a numerical framework based on the Lefschetz thimbles for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model. By introducing continuous auxiliary fields via the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, the partition function is formulated as a high-dimensional complex integral. We employ the complex Langevin equation to explore the saddle-point distribution of the effective action in the complex plane. Monte Carlo integration is then performed to compute the partition function and Green functions. Our numerical results exhibit excellent agreement with high-temperature expansions, infrared-limit solutions, and determinantal quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) simulations, confirming the validity of our framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our complex Langevin search successfully captures the relevant dominant saddle points governing the SYK model in the large-N limit. Our work deepens the understanding of the sign problem in the SYK model and provides a viable non-perturbative avenue for addressing sign problems in more complex strongly correlated systems.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Decoding SO(5) Deconfined Multicriticality: Conformal Bootstrap and Fuzzy-Sphere Spectroscopy
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Zhijin Li, Tinghong Shen
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: The nature of the deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) remains unsettled: competing explanations invoke a real multicritical conformal field theory (CFT) or pseudocriticality governed by nearby complex fixed points. We use the conformal bootstrap and fuzzy-sphere regularization to compute $SO(5)$ CFT data and compare our results with large-scale quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) data to investigate these scenarios. Using mixed correlators of the lowest vector $φ$, singlet $s$, and traceless symmetric scalar $t$, we characterize the bootstrap cone whose tip lies remarkably close to the position indicated by large-scale QMC. We extract an extensive spectrum across $SO(5)$ irreducible representations, together with operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients. We study a fuzzy-sphere realization of the $SO(5)$ nonlinear sigma model with a level-1 Wess--Zumino--Witten term. Using the special conformal generators, we identify 52 conformal primaries in a system with \(N=10\) Landau orbitals, including 31 not previously classified as primaries in the earlier fuzzy-sphere study. Symmetry projection extends fuzzy-sphere exact diagonalization to $N=12$. The bootstrap spectrum and OPE coefficients show close agreement with fuzzy-sphere data, including 16 of the newly identified primaries in channels accessible to the mixed-correlator bootstrap. The lowest $SO(5)$ singlet scalar is relevant in the bootstrap and QMC results; its fuzzy-sphere data is $Δ_s=2.816$ at $N=12$ and decreases with system size. Our results suggest that the mixed-correlator bootstrap solution represents a unitary CFT with a relevant $SO(5)$ singlet scalar and is closely connected to the QMC and fuzzy-sphere data for the DQCP. The conformal bootstrap, fuzzy-sphere, and QMC together provide comprehensive evidence for an $SO(5)$ multicritical CFT and critical data to decode the phases in two-dimensional quantum magnets.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Micromagnetic modelling and simulation of inertial magnetization dynamics in ferromagnets
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Massimiliano d'Aquino
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Magnetization dynamics at sub-picosecond time scales can exhibit inertial effects beyond the conventional Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert description, giving rise to nutational motion at terahertz frequencies. Following its theoretical prediction and experimental observation in ferromagnets, magnetic inertia has attracted increasing interest for understanding and controlling ultrafast spin dynamics. In this topical review, we discuss the theoretical modelling and micromagnetic simulation of inertial magnetization dynamics in ferromagnetic nanostructures. Starting from the mechanical analogy underlying the inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, we introduce its spatially inhomogeneous micromagnetic formulation and discuss its main properties, including magnetization-length conservation, angular-momentum relaxation, and the generalized free-energy balance. We then review the linear dynamics of inertial spin waves, highlighting the coexistence of GHz precessional and THz nutational branches, the inertial redshift of precessional modes, spectral linewidths, and the effects of exchange, magnetostatic interactions, confinement, curvature and torsion. Particular attention is devoted to the large-wavenumber regime, where magnetic inertia leads to a finite limiting spin-wave propagation velocity. Finally, we address frequency- and time-domain micromagnetic simulation techniques for spatially nonuniform inertial dynamics, including geometric midpoint integrators preserving the fundamental constraints and energy properties of the continuous dynamics. Applications to the excitation and propagation of ultrashort nutational spin waves and ultrafast inertial magnetization switching illustrate the role of micromagnetic modelling in connecting inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert theory with experimentally accessible nanoscale magnetization dynamics.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Assessing the expressive power of a gauge-invariant PEPS ansatz across a topological phase transition
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Etsuko Itou, Tsuyoshi Okubo
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: We investigate the expressive power of the gauged Gaussian fermionic projected entangled pair state (GGFPEPS) ansatz, which is a manifestly gauge-invariant tensor network ansatz for $(2+1)$-dimensional lattice gauge theories. In the GGFPEPS ansatz, the gauge field on each link is represented by coupling its configuration to the fermion number of virtual fermions placed at both ends of the link. This ansatz has been studied by variational Monte Carlo (VMC) methods in previous work~\cite{Emonts:2022yom}. However, the statistical error of VMC makes a precise determination of the variational parameters difficult, so that the expressive power of the ansatz could not be examined accurately. In this work, we reformulate the computation as a Grassmann tensor network (TN), in which the whole network is contracted deterministically, and introduce the higher-order tensor renormalization group (HOTRG), which allows us to perform calculations in large volumes up to $L=34$. We also evaluate the infinite volume system using the corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMRG). We find that the ansatz with only eight complex variational parameters accurately describes the pure $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory including the region of the topological phase transition, not only in the energy but also in the topological entanglement entropy. The critical coupling obtained from the peaks of their susceptibilities agrees quantitatively with the one predicted by continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo simulations~\cite{wu2012phase}. Furthermore, near the transition point, we show that the ansatz represents a state outside the plaquette product family, which is a one-parameter family of states assumed in the construction of the ansatz as a simple interpolation between the strong and weak coupling limits.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Uncovering the Structural, Electronic, and Electrostatic Landscapes of SrTiO$_3$ Grain Boundaries via Grand Canonical Monte Carlo with a Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Xing He, Kairi Masuda, Aaron M. Schankler, Songsong Zhou, Andrew M. Rappe
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Grain boundaries in perovskites exhibit a rich variety of electronic, polar and magnetic properties, yet identifying their atomic structures and compositions remains challenging. Here, we combine the Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) method with a universal machine-learning interatomic potential to explore the coupled compositional and structural phase space of $Σ$5(310)[001] SrTiO$_3$ grain boundaries. The resulting chemical potential phase diagram identifies ten stable structures belonging to four motif families: large Sr kite, small Sr kite, incomplete Sr large kite, and Ti-rich structures. Extending the GCMC method to the Sigma5(210)[001] and Sigma17(410)[001] grain boundaries reveals how grain boundary plane and inclination angle influence the competition between small- and large-kite motifs. Density functional theory calculations of the predicted Sigma5(310)[001] grain boundaries show that the composition and atomic structure strongly govern the spatial distribution of conduction and valence band edge states, interfacial band alignment, and carrier localization. Four distinct electronic regimes emerge: localized electron-doped, delocalized electron-doped, insulating, and hole-attracting states. Our electrostatics analysis reveals the coexistence of the short-range electric fields at the reconstructed GB core associated with local atomic density and bonding, and the longer-range fields outside the core arising from the space charge. These fields can also couple to local polar distortions and generate composition-dependent polarization patterns. These results establish an efficient framework for exploring oxide perovskite grain boundary structures and reveal how stoichiometry and atomic reconstruction couple to electronic structure, electrostatics, and local polarization, providing a route toward predictive grain boundary engineering in functional perovskites.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Multi-reference variational states resolve stripe selection and local $d$-wave pairing in the Hubbard model
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Honghui Shang, Jinlong Yang
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Whether stripes compete with $d$-wave superconductivity or promote pairing through fluctuations remains unsettled in the two-dimensional Hubbard model. Using multi-reference neural variational auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (MR-nVAFQMC) at $U/t=8$, we superpose unpaired Slater determinants across stripe periods and domain-wall positions, reaching variational energies competitive with leading benchmarks on periodic lattices up to $32\times32$ sites. For cuprate next-nearest-neighbor hopping ($t'/t=-0.2$), diagonal hopping preserves electron-doped antiferromagnetism while kinetically frustrating hole motion into Yamada stripes with a dome of short-range connected $d$-wave pairing. At $1/8$ hole doping, hole delocalization across antiphase spin boundaries outweighs on-site repulsion, splitting the filled stripes of the pure model into half-filled walls with strong local pairing. Coherently delocalizing shifted walls strongly suppresses static charge modulation yet leaves short-range pairing unchanged, showing that local pairing is intrinsic to half-filled walls rather than driven by stripe fluctuations. Across intervening antiferromagnetic domains, however, pairing correlations become unresolved at one stripe period and beyond. Both parameter transfer to larger lattices without reoptimization and deep benchmark checkpoints retain stripe spin order without resolving long-range pairing, within uncertainties allowing weak superconductivity. Half-filled antiphase walls thus generate local $d$-wave pairs, whereas suppressing static stripe order alone yields no resolved coherence across stripes in the states studied.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Atomically Sharp Magnetic Domain Walls beyond Micromagnetics
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Guokai Liao, Stefan Blügel
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Atomically narrow magnetic domain walls can arise in ultrathin magnetic films, van der Waals magnets, and systems with reduced effective exchange stiffness due to competing exchange interactions. As their width approaches the atomic lattice spacing, the continuum approximation underlying micromagnetics becomes increasingly unreliable. We investigate the structure and stability of such domain walls in a one-dimensional nearest-neighbor J-K-D spin-lattice model incorporating Heisenberg exchange, uniaxial anisotropy, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI). In the absence of DMI, we demonstrate analytically a continuous transition to an atomically sharp easy-axis wall at the critical exchange-to-anisotropy ratio J/K = 3/2, characterized by the softening of a localized Hessian mode. Atomistic spin-dynamics simulations confirm this transition and reveal that fitting discrete wall profiles with the conventional micromagnetic solution, as commonly done in experimental analyses, underestimates the exchange interaction and overestimates the anisotropy. Finite DMI removes the perfectly collinear wall as a stationary configuration, replacing the transition by a smooth crossover toward a strongly localized but canted wall that approaches the collinear easy-axis configuration only asymptotically in the strong-anisotropy limit. We derive an analytical expression for the DMI-induced canting in this regime and demonstrate its strongly enhanced canting response near the critical ratio. These findings establish the limitations of micromagnetic descriptions of atomically narrow domain walls and suggest opportunities for controlling their structure through anisotropy and DMI.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Benchmarking the accuracy of superconducting pair-pair correlations within constrained-path quantum Monte Carlo
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Jodie Roberts, Beau A. Thompson, R. Torsten Clay

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Quantum resources and the onset of the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Naga Dileep Varikuti, Leela Ganesh Chandra Lakkaraju, Philipp Hauke
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: The Monte Carlo sign problem poses a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet its connection to quantum resources remains poorly understood. We probe this connection by systematically tuning the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. In numerical tensor-network studies, we find the sign complexity and the quantum resources of entanglement and nonstabilizerness of the ground state to be strongly suppressed in a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity. As nonstoquasticity is further increased, the considered quantum resources experience sharp crossovers into a regime where they are strongly enhanced. Surprisingly, numerical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations drastically deteriorate in the same region, even though the Hamiltonian is already considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating that the failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than the sign structure of the Hamiltonian. We corroborate these findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state of k-local Hamiltonians in the stoquastic limit. Moreover, we identify a distinct behaviour in graph states. Their nonstabilizerness always vanishes, but, as we demonstrate analytically, on bipartite graphs the sign can be easily cured while in multipartite graph states it cannot. Our results thus shed light on the highly subtle interplay between quantum resources and the computational difficulty encountered by QMC methods.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Topological signatures of criticality: the Ising case
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Tak-Shing Chan, Paweł Dłotko, Jacek Gulgowski, Biagio Lucini, Mateusz Masłowski, Davide Vadacchino
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Topological properties of microscopic configurations may provide additional insight into phase transitions beyond conventional thermodynamic observables. We investigate this idea in the two-dimensional Ising model on square and triangular lattices by associating cell complexes with the positive and negative spin domains and constructing an Euler-characteristic observable from their difference. We provide the expression relating this quantity to conventional observables of the Ising model. This derivation allows us to understand its expected behavior physically. As a byproduct, we show that at any finite positive temperature the expectation of the Euler characteristic exceeds a positive, lattice-size-independent bound, hence disproving a previously suggested conjecture. Monte Carlo simulations combined with multihistogram reweighting show that this spin-odd topological observable exhibits order-parameter-like behavior near the ferromagnetic transition. Finite-size scaling of its susceptibility yields pseudocritical temperatures that converge to the known critical temperature for both lattice geometries. On the square lattice, the leading-order estimate of the critical exponent obtained from the topological observable depends more strongly on the fitting range than the magnetization estimate. This behavior is consistent with stronger subleading finite-size corrections, as supported by fits including an additional correction term. On the triangular lattice, the corresponding estimate remains consistent with the theoretical Ising value. Our study suggests that topologically defined quantities such as the Euler characteristic can provide an alternative way to locate order-disorder phase transitions in the systems considered here. Since the definition of these observables is purely geometrical, they can provide useful insights in cases in which order parameters cannot be constructed.

Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.title: Scalable Bayesian Optimization for Efficient Exploration of Moire Patterns
Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.authors: Panagiotis Krokidas, Christos Lazaridis, Vassilis Sioros, Efi-Maria Papia, Vassilios Constantoudis, George Giannakopoulos
Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.abstract: Large materials design spaces often contain rare high-performing configurations that are difficult to identify through trial-and-error exploration or purely representative machine-learning (ML) sampling. In this work, we present FruBO, a flexible Bayesian Optimization framework for accelerating the discovery of optimal configurations in computationally demanding materials design problems. As a case study, we investigate multilayer Moiré patterns generated by the superposition of six rotated hexagonal lattices, where the objective is to identify the rotational conformation that maximizes pore-size uniformity, quantified using the Jain fairness index. The resulting benchmark contains 600,000 unique configurations and exhibits a highly skewed objective distribution, making the global optimum difficult to locate by random sampling. We compare random exploration, Gaussian Process-based Bayesian Optimization, and Bayesian Optimization using a lightweight CatBoost surrogate with committee-based uncertainty estimation. Random sampling identifies the global optimum only after 533,012 evaluations, requiring approximately 31 hours, while Gaussian Process-based BO becomes impractical due to GPU memory exhaustion after 290 acquired samples. In contrast, FruBO with CatBoost identifies the global optimum after 1,470 acquired samples and approximately 1.15 hours. These results demonstrate that scalable surrogate models can substantially improve the feasibility and efficiency of BO in large nanomaterials design spaces.

Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling
Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.authors: Weiheng Li, Zhiyao Jiang, Bai Song
Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.abstract: Embedded microfluidic cooling is a promising technology for dissipating the intense heat generated by high-performance electronic chips. However, the design and optimization of such coolers impose prohibitive computational costs when using conventional numerical solvers. Here, we present a parameterized physics-informed neural network (PINN) as a deep learning framework for rapidly and accurately predicting the thermohydraulic performance of embedded manifold microchannels. By incorporating four geometric dimensions along with three spatial coordinates as the network inputs, the proposed model enables multiphysics prediction across a continuous design space. Remarkably, our predicted velocity and temperature fields differ from finite-element simulations by relative errors of only 8.1% and 5.6%, respectively, while reducing the computational time and cost by over four orders of magnitude. Key to this framework is a composite strategy combining geometric ansatz embedding, the SOAP optimizer, and a thermal-conductivity-based curriculum learning scheme, which helps overcome the convergence challenges inherent in training PINNs for complex three-dimensional flows. Notably, by leveraging a highly optimized JAX backend, the network achieves convergence on a single consumer-grade GPU in less than four hours. Our approach offers a physics-consistent, real-time surrogate model that can substantially accelerate innovations in advanced microfluidic cooling of future electronics.

Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.title: Physics Informed Priors for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials with Uncertainty Quantification
Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.authors: George I. Simmons, Thomas D. Swinburne, Thomas Hudson, James R. Kermode
Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.abstract: Standard uncertainty quantification methods for machine learning interatomic potentials often fail to quantify the effects of model misspecification despite its prominence as a source of error. To combat this, misspecification-aware uncertainty schemes have been gaining attention, pointwise optimal parameter set regression (POPS-Regression) among them. However, no guarantees on the physicality of the posterior distribution are given and uncertainty estimates can be conservative compared to the true error. To combat this, we present a model misspecification aware scheme that builds on POPS-Regression by allowing users to specify physical priors that are enforced across the obtained ensemble of models. This allows the user to incorporate misspecification-aware uncertainties without compromising on physical properties. The scheme is applicable to any physical quantity that can be represented by a convex set of parameters and so is robust for a wide variety of static properties which can help inform dynamical simulations. Here, we demonstrate the scheme for phononic vibrations and elastic properties. The scheme is also applied to both linear and message-passing neural network potentials by exploiting the linearity available in both architectures; for neural network potentials we approximate the readout layer as a linear model based on fixed non-linear features. The versatility of the method provides an alternative to hand-crafted or active learning approaches to data-set construction to correct physical failures by adding data thus reducing the computational overhead for designing potentials for specific applications.

Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.title: Empirical machine learning for 3He spin-filter polarization decay
Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.authors: Gonzalo Pérez-Blasco, Alexandre Guillaudin, Javier Campo, Gabriel J. Cuello
Machine Learning & Bayesian Optimization.abstract: A lightweight, empirical machine-learning framework is presented for predicting the time evolution of the nuclear polarization of 3 He spin-filter cells under realistic neutron beamline conditions. The method bridges the gap between detailed microscopic modeling of polarization relaxation and purely heuristic correction schemes by combining supervised learning with basic physics-informed constraints on spin relaxation.
